PE 1600 - People, Power, Politics
Credits: 4
An introductory course that begins with an examination of the nature of power in different areas of human experience,
and then proceeds to look at power issues related to lawmaking, governmental institutions, and political participation
both inside and outside of those institutions. The course is intended to illustrate the various sources of power that
people possess to bring about political and social change. It draws on current events in order to better illustrate the
topics discussed.
Prerequisites
EC I
When Offered:
Periodically.
PE 1650 - Politics of Comics
Credits: 4
This course explores the art form and the politics of comics in terms of how they are produced and by whom, as well as
the texts themselves and how they are received. It encompasses comics of various genres of fiction (superhero, horror,
slice-of-life, humor, science fiction, etc.) as well as nonfiction. Topics include immigration and religion, sex
discrimination and feminist movements, racial discrimination and civil rights movements, war and post-traumatic
stress, disability and monstrousness, class and privilege and vigilantism, sexuality and gender, and adolescence and
identity.

PE 3100 - International Relations
Credits: 4
This course introduces students to basic concepts and theories of international relations. Particular

institutions and international law. The course explores how each individual is related to global
politics and encourages students to study and propose solutions to issues related to war and peace,
including foreign policy, national security and national interests versus international law.

conducting primary research, and practice with negotiation and public speaking.

PE 3435 - Intermediate Macroeconomics: Theory and Policy
Credits: 4
This course surveys short-run macroeconomic theories and stabilization policies in five parts.
Part I presents and critiques the principal non-Keynesian theories of output and employment, including the classical
model, the monetarist model, and the rational expectations and real business cycle models.
Part II develops the simple Keynesian model of output and employment.
Part III extends the Keynesian model by incorporating money, monetary policy, and the analysis of depression
economies.
Part IV applies the Keynesian framework to open economy macroeconomics, examining the international transmission
of booms and busts across countries.
Part V concludes with a comparative analysis of the global spread of the Great Recession (2007-2010) from the United
States to ten other major economies.
Prerequisites
PE 2430
When Offered:
Every spring

PE 3610 - Conflict and Revolution in the 20th Century

PE 3720 - Long Island: Economy, Environment and Society
Credits: 4
Most Americans now live in suburban areas like Long Island. Since the Second World War and the building of
Levittown, Long Island’s economy has been transformed from an agricultural area to a bedroom community. Its natural
amenity allowed the creation of a number of parks known world over. Since the seventies, the area has witnessed a
boom in commerce and lately, of office space. The course covers the past and recent changes in this region.

Credits: 4
This course examines issues involved in sustainable development and is designed as a broad survey covering the most
critical topics in environmental economics. The significant contribution that economic analysis can make in
understanding the nature of problems in sustainable development and in providing possible solutions is the central
focus of the course. Market failures are the cause of many of our most serious environmental problems but can be
remedied with economic tools. The role that economic and political institutions play in allocating natural resources is
examined. Students are exposed to a number of emerging sustainability issues including global warming and given
ample opportunities to develop their own perspective.

society, feminist legal theory, critical race theory, and queer legal theory.

PE 4470 - History of Economic Thought
Credits: 4
This course traces the evolution of economic thought from the sixteenth century to the emergence of modern
economics in the twentieth century. It examines seven major schools and representative thinkers whose ideas shaped
the foundations of economic analysis:
1. The Mercantilists - Thomas Mun, Gerard Malynes, Charles Davenant, Jean-Baptiste Colbert, William Petty.
2. The Physiocrats - François Quesnay, Anne-Robert-Jacques T urgot.
3. Forerunners of the Classical School - Dudley North, Richard Cantillon, David Hume.

PE 4580 - Origins of Capitalism
Credits: 4
This course explores the historical development of modern capitalism from its earliest roots to the eve of World War
I. The material is organized into five parts.
Part I surveys pre-capitalist societies, tracing Western Europe’s evolution from primitive communities through ancient
Greece and Rome, Western feudalism, and mercantilism.
Part II examines the world of the 1780s-just before the Industrial and French Revolutions transformed economic and
political life-and investigates the emergence of the “spirit of capitalism” between the fifteenth and eighteenth
centuries.
Part III analyzes Adam Smith’s account of the origins and nature of modern commercial society in The Wealth of
Nations (Books I and III) and contrasts it with the Marxist class interpretation advanced by Marx and Engels in The
Communist Manifesto.
Part IV surveys the Industrial Revolution in Britain and its diffusion to France, Germany, the United States, and Japan.
Part V concludes with contrasting interpretations of mature capitalism in V . I. Lenin’s Imperialism: The Highest Stage of
Capitalism and J. M. Keynes’s The Economic Consequences of the Peace.
Prerequisites

PE 4600 - Depression Economics: Lessons from the Great Depression and the Great
Recession
Credits: 4
This course studies depression economics-a recently revived branch of macroeconomics that seeks to understand the
causes and policy remedies for large, contagious, global collapses in output and employment. We will analyze the causes
and policy remedies for depressions by comparing and contrasting the Great Depression of the 1930s with the Great
Recession of 2008. The advantage of the comparative approach is that it will enable us to isolate important common
characteristics of these two depressions; the circumstances that made each of these crises unique; and it can provide
important lessons for thinking about how to prevent future depressions.
Prerequisites
PE 2420

sometimes for the better, sometimes for the worse. In this course, you will learn how to use the tools of microeconomics
and empirical analysis to study the taxing and the spending activities of government. Some topics covered in this class
will include issues of social security, health insurance, income distribution and welfare programs, externalities and
public good, and taxation.
PE 4620 - Political & Social Thought
Credits: 4
Examines significant contributions to the development of western political thought from the Greeks to the 19th century.
Explores in depth works by Plato, Machiavelli, Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau, Burke and John Stuart Mill.
Prerequisites
Upper-Division standing
When Offered:

PE 4650 - Topics in U.S. Politics
Credits: 4
This course examines current debates and divergent views on a wide range of economic, political, and social issues.
Prerequisites
PE 2650

Periodically.

Credits: 4

Constitution and of the actions of the other two branches, focusing on the distribution of

the federal government can force businesses to conduct themselves in certain ways vis-à-vis their
employees and customers; the limits of citizens’ liberties of free speech, religious worship, and
privacy; and whether public or private organizations can exclude people based on race, class,
gender, or sexuality.
Prerequisites
Upper-Division standing
When Offered:
Periodically.
PE 4658 - Law and Civil Liberties
Credits: 4
This course is about your freedoms from government. It examines the historical evolution and
philosophical and political underpinnings of constitutional civil liberties. We will analyze Supreme
Court cases on such topics as speech, press, religion, privacy, searches, self-incrimination, counsel,
trials, bail, and the death penalty-how do they affect what we can say and when and where, how we
practice religion, how we make choices about our bodies, how we choose partners and form
families, how we are policed and processed and punished. We will apply this knowledge to current
events and policies, and assess their impact on the various groups in the United States.
Prerequisites
Upper-Division standing

Periodically.

independence movements. Major emphasis will be placed on post-independence politics, social and economic change.

records.title: People, Power, Politics
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
An introductory course that begins with an examination of the nature of power in different areas of human experience,
and then proceeds to look at power issues related to lawmaking, governmental institutions, and political participation
both inside and outside of those institutions. The course is intended to illustrate the various sources of power that
people possess to bring about political and social change. It draws on current events in order to better illustrate the
topics discussed.
Prerequisites
EC I
When Offered:
Periodically.

records.title: Politics of Comics
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course explores the art form and the politics of comics in terms of how they are produced and by whom, as well as
the texts themselves and how they are received. It encompasses comics of various genres of fiction (superhero, horror,
slice-of-life, humor, science fiction, etc.) as well as nonfiction. Topics include immigration and religion, sex
discrimination and feminist movements, racial discrimination and civil rights movements, war and post-traumatic
stress, disability and monstrousness, class and privilege and vigilantism, sexuality and gender, and adolescence and
identity.

Note:
Cross-listed as WS 1540 - duplicate all course information incl. pre-reqs, gen eds, course description.

records.title: Introduction to Law
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course is intended to familiarize students with the basic substantive, procedural, and structural components of the
legal system of the United States of America. This course provides an introduction to the common law and the essential
characteristics of the United States legal system: basic constitutional structures and the judicial function, the basics of
legal methodology, the role of the legal profession in an adversary system and a survey of core legal principles in
different areas of the law.
Prerequisites
EC I
When Offered:
Every semester.

records.title: Principles of Microeconomics
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
An introduction to neoclassical economic theory. Consumer and producer behaviors, price formation in the market and
the role of the market in allocating resources and coordinating social production are among the topics covered.
Prerequisites
ECI
When Offered:
Every semester

records.title: Principles of Macroeconomics
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4

An introduction to conventional macroeconomic theory, including the determination of national income, government
taxing and spending policy, money and banking, unemployment, and inflation.
Prerequisites
EC I
When Offered:
Every semester

records.title: Introduction to U.S. Politics
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This introduction to power and politics in the U.S. explores the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution;
public opinion, interest groups, social movements, and voting; the institutions of Congress, the Presidency and the
Supreme Court; and the making of current policies. Emphasis is placed on issues of power, democracy, and political and
social change.
Prerequisites
EC I
When Offered:
Every semester.

records.title: Introduction to Urban Issues
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
An examination of various perspectives on urban areas and of important urban issues, including social problems of
minority communities, housing and public services.
Prerequisites
EC I
When Offered:
Periodically

records.title: International Relations
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course introduces students to basic concepts and theories of international relations. Particular
focus is given to historical patterns of continuity and change in world politics and the evolution of
world orders, including great power relations, geopolitics, and, thus, the evolution of international
institutions and international law. The course explores how each individual is related to global
politics and encourages students to study and propose solutions to issues related to war and peace,
including foreign policy, national security and national interests versus international law.
Prerequisites
ECII
When Offered:
Every semester.

records.title: Model United Nations
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
The course prepares students for a Model United Nations conference where students perform the role of a diplomat
from an assigned country. Students acquire a working knowledge of the United Nations, a familiarity with current
issues on the international agenda, an in -depth knowledge of an assigned country, an unparalleled experience in
conducting primary research, and practice with negotiation and public speaking.
Prerequisites
EC11 and instructor’s approval
When Offered:
Every spring semester.

records.title: Ethnicity and Race in Global Perspective
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4

This course explores identity politics across the world focusing on ethnicity, race, and nationalism.
We will survey theories of identity and examine their contemporary practices. Topics include
nation-building and state-building; identity, imperialism, and anti-imperialism; identity politics and
conflict; and multiculturalism.
Prerequisites
EC II
When Offered:
Periodically

records.title: Statistics
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Surveys the basic topics of modern statistics, including descriptive statistics, probability theory, probability distributions,
hypothesis testing, simple regression.
Prerequisites
MA 1020

records.title: United States Economic History
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course provides a comprehensive introduction to the economic history of the United States. It covers the
development of the U.S. economy from colonial times through the neoliberal counterrevolution. Topics include settler
colonialism, slavery, proletarianization, industrialization, class conflict, crisis and more.
Prerequisites
NoneCorequisite NonePrerequisite/Corequisite
None
When Offered:

OtherNote:
None

records.title: Inter-American Relations and Immigration
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course examines the political, economic, and social processes that shape foreign policies and international relations
in the Western Hemisphere, and the consequences of those policies and relationships for the peoples of the hemisphere.
The main themes include manifest destiny, imperialism, the Cold War, neoliberalism, and inter- American immigration.
Prerequisites
ECII
When Offered:
Every other Spring.

records.title: Topics in Latin American Politics
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course examines the political and economic similarities and differences in subregions of Latin
America (such as the Spanish-speaking Caribbean, Central America, Andean nations). It explores
the shared histories and particular experiences in domestic development, international relations,
and integration in the global economy, and analyzes contemporary debates on a wide range of
issues including inequality, authoritarianism vs. democracy, population migrations, and the impact
of climate crisis. Subregions and themes vary and are announced at the time the class is posted
for registration.
Prerequisites
EC II
When Offered:
Periodically.

records.title: Global South
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Analysis of major political, economic and social problems of the Global South (i.e. nations of Africa, Asia, Latin America,
and the Caribbean). The course broadly traces the history of colonialism and considers its impact on the post-colonial
political economy of the Global South. Case studies may complement the general analysis.
Prerequisites
ECII
When Offered:
Every semester

records.title: Contemporary U.S. Political Economy
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course is designed to familiarize the student with the workings of the economy within a class and institutional
context. Focuses on the economic history of the United States from the perspective of competition between firms,
management/worker relations and the involvement of the state in the economy.
Prerequisites
ECII
When Offered:
Every semester.

records.title: Intermediate Microeconomics
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
An in‑depth study of price theory. Develops and redefines the neoclassical principles presented in PE 2420
. Emphasizes the application of economic theory to public policy making.
Prerequisites
PE 2420 (minimum C-)

When Offered:
Every semester

records.title: Intermediate Macroeconomics: Theory and Policy
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course surveys short-run macroeconomic theories and stabilization policies in five parts.
Part I presents and critiques the principal non-Keynesian theories of output and employment, including the classical
model, the monetarist model, and the rational expectations and real business cycle models.
Part II develops the simple Keynesian model of output and employment.
Part III extends the Keynesian model by incorporating money, monetary policy, and the analysis of depression
economies.
Part IV applies the Keynesian framework to open economy macroeconomics, examining the international transmission
of booms and busts across countries.
Part V concludes with a comparative analysis of the global spread of the Great Recession (2007-2010) from the United
States to ten other major economies.
Prerequisites
PE 2430
When Offered:
Every spring

records.title: International Economics
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
The focus of this course is international trade theory and policy. It covers as well certain fundamental aspects of
international monetary economics. The curriculum is designed to provide students with the basic skills required for an
understanding and critical analysis of the principal global economic issues facing the United States and the world today.
Prerequisites

PE 2420
or PE 2430
When Offered:
Periodically.

records.title: Women from a Global Perspective
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course examines the various roles of women in the global economy, with particular emphasis on the international
division of labor. It provides a class, ethnic and historical analysis of the study of women as part of economic and social
change. Case studies of women in advanced capitalist and Third World nations show their increasing interactions.
Prerequisites
ECII
When Offered:
Periodically.

records.title: Economics of Sports
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course examines the economics of professional sports and sporting activities, and their role in regional economic
growth. The focus of the course is on practical applications of economic theory to problems related to these industries.
Students are expected to be able to define key concepts as well as demonstrate the ability to use analytical tools to solve
problems illustrative of issues related to sports and sports industry concerns such as: Identify the basic economic factors
affecting professional sports. Use rudimentary economic models to examine the economic impact of professional sports
activities, and their interrelationship with other economic activities. Understand the basic methodology of economic
impact analysis. Identify and explain the economic principles and problems associated with sports team ownership.
Identify and explain the economic principles and problems associated with stadium economics. Explain the impact and
effects of radio and television broadcast rights on team ownership and profitability.
Prerequisites

Principles of Microeconomics or Principles of Macroeconomics
When Offered:
Other

records.title: Conflict and Revolution in the 20th Century
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Rapid changes in the global economy, the rise of 20th Century social movements as well as ethnic tensions have led to
conflicts in various parts of the world. The different origins of the violence as well as the outcomes are the subject matter
of this course. Case studies including the Middle East, Africa, Latin America and the Caribbean, China and the U.S. Civil
Rights movements are used selectively to illustrate instances of rebellion.
Prerequisites
ECII

records.title: City & Suburb: Political Action and Change
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
A survey of city and suburban organization practices. Examines the role of the community organization in fostering
local autonomy and as an agency for social, political and economic change in our cities and suburbs.
Prerequisites
ECII

records.title: Long Island: Economy, Environment and Society
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Most Americans now live in suburban areas like Long Island. Since the Second World War and the building of
Levittown, Long Island’s economy has been transformed from an agricultural area to a bedroom community. Its natural
amenity allowed the creation of a number of parks known world over. Since the seventies, the area has witnessed a
boom in commerce and lately, of office space. The course covers the past and recent changes in this region.

Prerequisites
ECII

records.title: Politics of Race and Class
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course explores the intersection of race and class in the U.S., inquires into the relationship between race and quality
of life, and examines limitations on the representativeness of the political system at federal, state, and local levels of
government. Central to the course is the question of government responsiveness on issues of race and class. Particular
attention is paid to the operation of U.S. political parties, to elections and voting, to legislative process and executive
leadership, and to media performance in public debate.
Prerequisites
EC II

records.title: State and Local Politics
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
The course examines government and politics at the state and local level, with particular emphasis on New York State. It
discusses issues in state and local government and the impact of the competing interests of the people of New York on
public policy. It also explores the historical context and contemporary state of policy initiatives on issues such as
criminal justice, welfare, health care, education, immigration, the environment and taxation.
Prerequisites
ECII
When Offered:
Periodically.

records.title: Inequality and Mobility Through the Data: Empirical Methods in Social Policy
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4

This course builds on concepts across PEL majors with a focus on applying data and empirical methods to social policy.
Students will gain experience working with data to explore geographic and intergenerational patterns in inequality and
mobility, in both upper- and lower-income countries. Through applications of observational and experimental causal
inference methods, students will learn how to identify and articulate clear policy questions, propose concrete solutions,
and evaluate the effectiveness of social programs. Because the course focuses more on applications than on theory,
students are encouraged to enroll even if they have not taken a course in econometrics.
Prerequisites
NoneCorequisite NonePrerequisite/Corequisite
None
When Offered:
OtherNote:
None

records.title: International Organizations in the Global Economy
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course explores various approaches to international organizations and the contribution these organizations make to
the creation, maintenance, and change of world order. Current issues facing the United Nations and its specialized
agencies, the Bretton Woods financial institutions, and regional organizations will be examined. While much attention is
given in this course to the role of permanent, intergovernmental organizations, the course also examines the role of
nongovernmental organizations, international law, treaties, and norms in international relations.
Prerequisites
Upper-Division standing

records.title: Middle Eastern Politics
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Recent events like the terrorist attacks of September the 11th, the Persian Gulf Wars, the U.S. occupation of Iraq, the
Arab-Israeli conflict, the rise of political Islam have highlighted awareness of the significance of the Middle East in
world politics as well as the lack of understanding about the region in the West. This course explores the geographic,

historical, political, economic, and cultural aspects of the Middle East, covering such topics as the making of the modern
Middle East, Arab nationalism, the U.S. occupation of Iraq, the Palestinian-Israeli conflict, Islam and human/women’s
rights, and Iran and the bomb.
Prerequisites
Upper-Division standing

records.title: Applied Econometrics
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Builds on the knowledge and skills in statistics by the study of simple and multiple regression analysis to test empirical
propositions in economics and to forecast economic time series. Students are also required to become fluent in the use of
a statistics computer program.
Prerequisites
MA 2300
, MA 2310
, PE 3201

records.title: Environmental Politics
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
The course will begin by examining the crucial biophysical, economic, and social issues facing local communities and
political leaders today. In the second part of the course students are brought through the history, organizations, interests
groups, and processes that shape U.S. and international environmental policy. The latter will conclude with the current
debates that inform policies and negotiations within such institutions as the WTO, United Nations and agreements such
as NAFTA. Students will be assigned examples of communities that have confronted environmental problems and they
will research the processes by which those communities addressed them.
Prerequisites

Upper-Division standing

records.title: Environmental Economics
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course examines issues involved in sustainable development and is designed as a broad survey covering the most
critical topics in environmental economics. The significant contribution that economic analysis can make in
understanding the nature of problems in sustainable development and in providing possible solutions is the central
focus of the course. Market failures are the cause of many of our most serious environmental problems but can be
remedied with economic tools. The role that economic and political institutions play in allocating natural resources is
examined. Students are exposed to a number of emerging sustainability issues including global warming and given
ample opportunities to develop their own perspective.
Prerequisites
PE 2420
or PE 2430

records.title: Jurisprudence: Legal Thought
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course is a survey of major theoretical approaches to the nature, purposes, interpretation, and practice of law.
Through primary classical and contemporary documents, we will explore “classical” legal philosophies such as natural
law and legal positivism, as well as the more “modern” theories of American legal thought: legal realism, law and
society, feminist legal theory, critical race theory, and queer legal theory.
Prerequisites
Upper-Division standing

records.title: Urban Economics
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4

This course examines the evolution of cities and metropolitan areas as centers of production and the relationship of
urban economics to regional, national, and international economics. Attention is paid to the failure to meet the needs of
significant numbers of people in urban areas.
Prerequisites
Upper-Division standing
When Offered:
Periodically.

records.title: Health Economics
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Health Economics provides a broad overview of healthcare delivery and finance systems, both in the U.S. and abroad,
and explores the role that economic theory plays in the national healthcare reform debate. The student will be
introduced to a number of basic theoretical tools used in economics to explain the allocation of scarce resources in
healthcare markets. The course will also explore a number of controversial questions involving the rationing of care,
“market failures” in the current healthcare system, disparities in access to care, and the extent to which recent healthcare
reform legislation addresses these issues.
Prerequisites
Upper Division Standing

records.title: Food and Wine Economics
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
The purpose of this course is to provide students with a systematic introduction to basic economic concepts and issues
as they relate to the food and wine industry. The process requires an understanding of the microeconomic and
macroeconomic forces influencing the decisions of producers and consumers. Topics include supply and demand of
food and wine, food and wine production function, both under perfect and imperfect competition as well as an
introduction to behavioral economics. The course also addresses concepts in natural resources such as the tragedy of the
commons and externalities, as well as government programs.

Prerequisites
PE 2420

records.title: The Politics of Gender and Sexuality
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course examines how constructed norms of “gender” and “sexuality” have shaped our
identities, our opportunities, our media representations, and our laws, and how we can re-construct
those norms to make change in these areas as well. We will explore topics such as child rearing and
abortion, non-marital sex, work and income, sexual harassment, interpersonal violence, sexual as‐
sault, and dating and marriage. We will investigate how
women, people of color, people who are working class or in poverty, people who identify as
LGBTQ+, and people who are unmarried have been particularly subject to discrimination in these
areas, and how movements for equality have challenged this discrimination and pushed for social
justice.
Prerequisites
Upper Division Standing

records.title: Economic Development
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
A comparative study of economic development strategies and problems of Third World countries. The course will locate
the application of development strategies in different institutional and political settings. The implication of debt
repayment on economic development will also be examined.
Prerequisites
PE2420 or PE2430.

records.title: International Finance
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Surveys three areas: international financial markets; open-economy macroeconomics; and international monetary
systems and policy. Specific topics include position taking, arbitrage, parity conditions, international banking, monetary
and fiscal policy, capital mobility, fixed and flexible exchange rates, the gold standard, Bretton Woods, and the current
“free market” international monetary order.
Prerequisites
PE 2430

records.title: History of Economic Thought
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course traces the evolution of economic thought from the sixteenth century to the emergence of modern
economics in the twentieth century. It examines seven major schools and representative thinkers whose ideas shaped
the foundations of economic analysis:
1. The Mercantilists - Thomas Mun, Gerard Malynes, Charles Davenant, Jean-Baptiste Colbert, William Petty.
2. The Physiocrats - François Quesnay, Anne-Robert-Jacques T urgot.
3. Forerunners of the Classical School - Dudley North, Richard Cantillon, David Hume.

4. The Principal Classical Economists - Adam Smith, Thomas Robert Malthus, David Ricardo.
5. Interpreters of the Classical Tradition - John Stuart Mill, Karl Marx.
6. Modern Microeconomics - William Stanley Jevons, Alfred Marshall.
7. Modern Macroeconomics - John Maynard Keynes.
The course emphasizes the historical context in which these theories arose and their continuing relevance to
contemporary economic analysis and policy debates.
Prerequisites
PE2420 and PE2430 or Upper Division Standing/Permission from Instructor
When Offered:
Every spring

records.title: Origins of Capitalism
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course explores the historical development of modern capitalism from its earliest roots to the eve of World War
I. The material is organized into five parts.
Part I surveys pre-capitalist societies, tracing Western Europe’s evolution from primitive communities through ancient
Greece and Rome, Western feudalism, and mercantilism.
Part II examines the world of the 1780s-just before the Industrial and French Revolutions transformed economic and
political life-and investigates the emergence of the “spirit of capitalism” between the fifteenth and eighteenth
centuries.
Part III analyzes Adam Smith’s account of the origins and nature of modern commercial society in The Wealth of
Nations (Books I and III) and contrasts it with the Marxist class interpretation advanced by Marx and Engels in The
Communist Manifesto.
Part IV surveys the Industrial Revolution in Britain and its diffusion to France, Germany, the United States, and Japan.
Part V concludes with contrasting interpretations of mature capitalism in V . I. Lenin’s Imperialism: The Highest Stage of
Capitalism and J. M. Keynes’s The Economic Consequences of the Peace.
Prerequisites

PE2420 and PE2430 or Upper Division Standing/Permission from Instructor
When Offered:
Every fall

records.title: Global Economy in the 20th Century
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course analyzes political and economic change in selected countries of the region from the mid-twentieth century to
the present. It examines the impact of foreign control over local resources, uneven capitalist development, class conflict,
and the contemporary “pink tide” of new governments on poverty, inequality, and social progress.
Prerequisites
PE 3410
, or PE 2420
, or PE 2430
, or upper division standing
When Offered:
Every other Spring.

records.title: Depression Economics: Lessons from the Great Depression and the Great
records.sourceText:
Recession
Credits: 4
This course studies depression economics-a recently revived branch of macroeconomics that seeks to understand the
causes and policy remedies for large, contagious, global collapses in output and employment. We will analyze the causes
and policy remedies for depressions by comparing and contrasting the Great Depression of the 1930s with the Great
Recession of 2008. The advantage of the comparative approach is that it will enable us to isolate important common
characteristics of these two depressions; the circumstances that made each of these crises unique; and it can provide
important lessons for thinking about how to prevent future depressions.
Prerequisites
PE 2420
or PE 2430

or Upper Division Standing
When Offered:
Every two years.

records.title: Public Administration
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Examines organizational theories and their application in public policy. Focuses on how decisions made at various levels
of government are implemented in local urban and non‑urban areas. The course involves field work, visiting public
offices and contacting interviews of role players in public administration case study projects.
Prerequisites
Upper-Division standing
When Offered:
Periodically.

records.title: Political Power and Social Class
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course analyzes the interaction of political power and social class from two vantage points–power from above and
power from below. The first part of the course considers pluralist and conflict theories of the relationship between the
state and society. The second part focuses on social movement theories, using cases from various parts of the world to
illustrate effective challenges to entrenched political power as well as obstacles faced by people who feel excluded from
institutions and structures of power.
Prerequisites
Upper-Division standing

records.title: Public Finance and Public Policy
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4

Public finance (also known as public economics) analyzes the impact of public policy on the allocation of resources and
the distribution of income in the economy. Government affects almost everything that we do in our daily lives,
sometimes for the better, sometimes for the worse. In this course, you will learn how to use the tools of microeconomics
and empirical analysis to study the taxing and the spending activities of government. Some topics covered in this class
will include issues of social security, health insurance, income distribution and welfare programs, externalities and
public good, and taxation.

records.title: Political & Social Thought
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Examines significant contributions to the development of western political thought from the Greeks to the 19th century.
Explores in depth works by Plato, Machiavelli, Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau, Burke and John Stuart Mill.
Prerequisites
Upper-Division standing
When Offered:
Every other semester.

records.title: Topics in U.S. Politics
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course examines current debates and divergent views on a wide range of economic, political, and social issues.
Prerequisites
PE 2650
or Upper-Division standing
When Offered:
Periodically.

records.title: Constitutional Law and Politics
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4

This course examines the judicial branch of government as the chief interpreter of the U.S.
Constitution and of the actions of the other two branches, focusing on the distribution of
constitutional power among the three branches, and between the national government and the
states. We will look at such issues as legislative and executive powers in wartime; whether states or
the federal government can force businesses to conduct themselves in certain ways vis-à-vis their
employees and customers; the limits of citizens’ liberties of free speech, religious worship, and
privacy; and whether public or private organizations can exclude people based on race, class,
gender, or sexuality.
Prerequisites
Upper-Division standing
When Offered:
Periodically.

records.title: Law and Civil Liberties
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course is about your freedoms from government. It examines the historical evolution and
philosophical and political underpinnings of constitutional civil liberties. We will analyze Supreme
Court cases on such topics as speech, press, religion, privacy, searches, self-incrimination, counsel,
trials, bail, and the death penalty-how do they affect what we can say and when and where, how we
practice religion, how we make choices about our bodies, how we choose partners and form
families, how we are policed and processed and punished. We will apply this knowledge to current
events and policies, and assess their impact on the various groups in the United States.
Prerequisites
Upper-Division standing
When Offered:
Periodically.

records.title: Law and Civil Rights
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course is about your right to be treated equally. It examines the historical evolution and
philosophical and political underpinnings of your civil rights. We will analyze Supreme Court cases
and other writings on discrimination on the basis of race, ethnicity, gender, sexuality, class, age, and
disability, and discuss such topics as desegregation, affirmative action, voting, sex, marriage,
abortion, sexual harassment, immigration and citizenship, work, welfare, and education. We
will apply this knowledge to current events and policies, and assess their impact on the various
groups in the United States.
Prerequisites
Upper-Division standing
When Offered:
Periodically.

records.title: Politics of India and the Region
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Introduction to the politics of selected countries in the Indian subcontinent. The course will examine the origins of the
independence movements. Major emphasis will be placed on post-independence politics, social and economic change.
Prerequisites
Upper-Division standing
When Offered:
Periodically.

records.title: Human Rights
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course aims to provide students with a broad working knowledge of human rights as both an intellectual discourse
and a realm of political action. The course examines: the emergence and institutionalization of human rights in the 20th
century, human rights as a form of international politics, the difficulties in enforcing international standards as well as a

specific analysis of a number of human rights issues.
Prerequisites
Upper-Division standing
When Offered:
Periodically.

records.title: Politics of Latin America and the Caribbean
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course analyzes political and economic change in selected countries of the region from the mid-twentieth century to
the present. It examines the impact of foreign control over local resources, uneven capitalist development, class conflict,
and the contemporary “pink tide” of new governments on poverty, inequality, and social progress.
Prerequisites
Upper-Division standing
When Offered:
Every other Spring.

records.title: Internship
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This internship will give students practical experience in the fields of public policy, legal affairs, economics as well as
state and local governments. Students will be working in various public nonprofit advocacy agencies. The working
hours and duration of the internship will be determined by the instructor and the agency. Students will be required to
submit a journal and a portfolio of work at the end of the semester. This is an excellent opportunity for students to
acquire training in their chosen area of specialization.
Prerequisites
Introductory courses in PEL and permission of the instructor

records.title: New York State Assembly Session Internship
records.sourceText:
Credits: 15
This is a fifteen-credit course that takes place in Albany every spring semester. It begins the first week of January and
runs through the middle of May. Students work approximately 30 hours per week in the office of a member of the New
York State Assembly and take one seminar course focusing on government and politics in New York State. The State
provides a stipend to assist with relocation and housing. Enrollment is by application and is competitive. Application
deadline: mid-October.
